fable-5.1.text:
So, the way I think about it, it's useful to first look at what scaling actually did for the field and why it was so attractive. If you go back to, let's say, 2012 to 2020, that was the age of research. People had lots of ideas, they tried different things, and the compute was small. Then the insight of scaling came along, and really it is a very simple insight. You take the pre-training recipe, next-token prediction on a very large amount of text, and you make the model bigger, the data bigger, the compute bigger, and you get a very predictable improvement. And this is an extremely attractive thing. It's a low-risk way to invest compute. You know that if you spend ten times more, you will get something better. It doesn't require you to have a new idea. So the whole industry organized itself around this word. Scaling became a kind of magic word that tells you exactly what to do.

But the thing about pre-training specifically is that the data is finite. It was a very particular situation. You happened to have this enormous amount of human text that nobody created for the purpose of training a neural network, and it turned out you could extract a tremendous amount of understanding from it. But at some point you've used it. And then the question becomes, what do you scale next?

So now you see people scaling RL. And I think RL is real, it does work. But it's different in character. With pre-training, the thing you were scaling was like a natural resource. It was just there. With RL you're constructing the environment, you're constructing the reward, and a lot of what you get depends on your choices there. So it's much less obvious that there is one quantity you turn up and get the same clean predictability. The compute is still very important, you cannot do anything without the compute. But I would say we are moving from a period where the recipe was known and the question was execution, back to a period where the question is, what is the recipe? What is the thing you should actually be scaling?

And I think there's a clue in the fact that the models do extremely well on all the evals, and yet the economic impact is lagging behind what the evals would suggest. That is telling you something. It's telling you that the way these models generalize is not like how a person generalizes. A person doesn't need a thousand examples to learn a new thing, and a person's performance on a test tells you quite a lot about how they'll do in the world. For these models that connection is weaker. And I don't think more of the same gets you that. So the way I'd put it is, scaling is still a tool, and you would never want to do research without the big computers. But I think we're back in an age of research. It's just the age of research with big computers.

opus-5.5.text:
So, one way I think about it is that "scaling" was a very powerful word, because it told people what to do. Up until around 2020, it was the age of research. People were trying all kinds of ideas and seeing what worked. Then from roughly 2020 to 2025, it was the age of scaling. People realized that if you take this recipe, pre-training, and add more compute, more data, and a bigger neural net, you get better results. That was extremely attractive, especially for companies, because it's a very low-risk way to invest resources. You know that if you put more in, you'll get something better out. Compare that to research, where you need to find good ideas and you don't know whether they'll work.

But pre-training has a particular property that made it so scalable: you don't have to think about what data to use. The answer is everything, all the text. That decision was made for you. Now the data is finite, and at some point it runs out. So the question becomes: what do you do next?

What's happening now is that people are trying to scale other things. Reinforcement learning is the obvious one. I believe people now spend more compute on RL than on pre-training, because RL runs are very long and each rollout is expensive and gives relatively little learning signal. But I'm not sure "scaling" is even the right frame for what comes next. With RL, you have to choose the environments and decide what to train on. There's a lot of freedom there, which means it's no longer a simple recipe where you add more and it gets better. You have to be thoughtful.

There are also ideas, like value functions, that could make this much more efficient. Right now, in naive RL, you only find out how well you did at the very end of a long trajectory. A value function lets you get a signal partway through, so you don't have to wait until the end to learn something. That's a good example of something that isn't "just scale it." It's an idea that makes the use of compute more productive.

So my view is that we're returning to the age of research, just with very big computers. Compute is large now. It's not clear that making it a hundred times bigger would transform everything. It would be different, of course, but the bottleneck is shifting back toward ideas. And I think the most important idea, the thing that matters most, is generalization. These models generalize dramatically worse than people. That's the core issue, and you won't solve it just by making things bigger.

fable-5.text:
One way to think about it is to ask: what is scaling? What does the word even mean? The thing that happened with pre-training is that people discovered a recipe. And the recipe had a very special property, which is that you could keep applying it and keep getting better results. You get more data, you get more compute, you train a bigger model on more data, and the model just gets better. And crucially, you knew it would get better in advance. That's what made it a recipe. It de-risked the investment. You could say, I'm going to spend this much on compute, and I have confidence that something good will come out.

So in some sense you could divide the history of the field into eras. From 2012 to maybe 2020, it was the age of research. People were trying different things, different architectures, different ideas. Then from 2020 onwards, it became the age of scaling. The word "scaling" became almost a magic word. You say the word, and the implication is, just make it bigger and everything will be better.

But here's the thing. Pre-training has a particular property, which is that the data is finite. There is only so much of it. It's a lot, it's a very large amount, but it is finite, and at some point you run into that. So then people move to other things — RL is the big one now — and they say, we are scaling RL, we are scaling inference-time compute. And those things also consume enormous amounts of compute, so in that sense it looks like scaling continues. But it's a different kind of thing. The RL environments are designed by people. Someone sits down and crafts them. It's less of a clean recipe where you turn the crank and know what comes out.

So my view is that we are, in some sense, moving back from the age of scaling to the age of research — but with one very big difference, which is that now the computers are big. In the past you had research with small computers. Now it's research with large computers. The question stops being "can you scale?" and goes back to being "what should you scale?" Because scaling, really, is just a way of asking: are you using your compute on the right thing? And I think finding the right thing — that's the research question again.

opus-5.text:
Scaling was the most important idea in AI, but I think its real significance was a little different from how people usually tell it. The significance was not just that bigger models are better. It's that for the first time, the field had a recipe and a knob. You could say to a very large number of people, "do this exact thing, but with a hundred times more compute," and it would work, and you could predict more or less how well it would work before you did it. That is an incredibly unusual situation in research. It means you don't need taste. You don't need to be lucky. You just need conviction and resources. And so an enormous amount of the activity of the last five years has been the pursuit of that, correctly, because it was the highest-return thing available.

But the thing about scaling is that you have to be scaling *something*. Pre-training had the beautiful property that the thing you scaled came for free — the data was just there, the internet existed, you didn't have to design it. And that's the part that runs out. Compute keeps growing, data does not, and so at some point the question changes from "how much do I scale" to "what do I scale," and that second question is not a scaling question. It's a research question again.

That's why I think we're going back to an age of research. With RL, you don't inherit an ocean of data; you have to build the environments, decide what's being rewarded, and you burn a lot of compute per unit of actual insight. There's no single knob.

The difference from 2015 is that now research happens with enormous compute, which is a genuinely different activity — and in some ways harder, because it's tempting to use compute as a substitute for understanding. But the actual gap seems to be something like generalization. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours. Our models see more driving data than any human ever could and are still worse at the long tail. Whatever accounts for that gap is not a quantity you turn up.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Scaling was a very powerful idea, but I think the word itself hides something important. When you say "scaling," you're really saying "find something to scale." Pre-training was the perfect thing to scale because it's a recipe: you put in a certain amount of compute and a certain amount of data, and you get predictable improvement. Everyone could trust it, and that's why it absorbed so much investment. It took very little thinking to see that it would work.

So the real question is what the next thing to scale is. RL and other post-training approaches are clearly consuming a lot of compute now, probably already comparable to pre-training or more. But it's much less obvious what the recipe is. With pre-training you didn't have to decide what the data was, because it was just everything people had written. With RL you have to choose environments and decide what the reward is. There's a lot of freedom, which also means a lot of ways to go wrong, and the returns for any given amount of compute are much harder to predict.

I'd also say we're moving from an age of scaling back toward an age of research. Scaling gave the field a comfortable answer: if you're not sure what to do, make it bigger. But if the data is finite, and pre-training will run out of data eventually, then just making it bigger stops being the whole story. You need new ideas about how to use the compute, and those ideas won't be obvious in the way the pre-training recipe was.

So I wouldn't say scaling is wrong. Scale is still enormously important. But "scaling" is no longer a complete strategy. You have to ask what you're scaling, and whether it's the most productive use of the compute. I think answering that will take real research, and it will matter more than people assume.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think scaling is still the right instinct, but it's no longer one thing. For a long time the recipe was simple: more compute, more data, bigger networks, and the loss kept going down in a predictable way. Pre-training gave us that. The trouble is that the data we can use is finite, so you can't keep scaling pre-training the same way forever. That pushes us to ask what else we can scale.

Reinforcement learning and test-time compute are the obvious candidates. They let a model spend more effort on a problem and be trained on outcomes rather than just imitating text. But I don't think we understand yet how to get the most out of them, and I'd be wary of treating "more RL compute" as a complete answer. A lot of what we'd want is generalization: a model that learns from far fewer examples and transfers what it learned to new situations, the way people do.

So I'd frame scaling as a question about which ingredients matter and how they interact, not as a single dial. The age of simply scaling everything may be ending, and that means research matters again. We have to find the ideas that make the scaling we already know about work better, rather than assuming bigger will be enough.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think scaling becomes useful once you have a learning process that reliably improves as you give it more resources. With pre-training, the resources are relatively easy to describe: you have more data, more compute, a larger model. And you can study how the results change.

Beyond pre-training, you need to establish that relationship again. Suppose you have a system that tries to solve problems, receives feedback, and learns from its attempts. You can spend more compute generating attempts. But how much does it learn from them? Can it keep finding problems that teach it something? How good is the feedback? Those become very consequential questions.

So I would think of scaling as a property you want your training method to have. You want additional resources to produce predictable improvements, ideally over a very large range. Finding a method with that property is itself a research problem. Once you have it, scaling gives you a powerful way to make progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful thing about scaling is that it turns a research result into a recipe. You find something that works at a small scale, and then you ask: if I put more compute into this, will it keep getting better? How reliably? And for how long?

Pre-training was a particularly powerful example because the recipe was relatively simple. You had a lot of data, you had an objective, and you could make progress by doing more of the same thing. But scaling itself doesn’t tell you what the next recipe should be. You still need the research that discovers it.

So, beyond pre-training, I would ask: what exactly are we scaling? If it’s reinforcement learning, for example, are we scaling the amount of experience? The difficulty of the problems? The variety of environments? Those choices matter. You can spend a lot of compute repeating something that no longer teaches the model very much.

The important thing is to find a process where additional computation continues to produce useful learning. Once you have that, scaling becomes extremely powerful. But finding that process is a scientific problem. You can’t replace that part simply by deciding to use more compute.

sol-6.text: I think scaling remains a useful framework, but we have to ask what is being scaled. In pre-training, it was relatively clear: more data, more compute, larger models. Beyond pre-training, the challenge is to create a training signal that rewards better reasoning and lets the model learn from its mistakes. If we can do that reliably, then more compute can continue to produce better systems. The difficult part is finding that signal, especially for problems where we can’t easily tell whether an answer is correct.

terra-5.6.text:
I think the key lesson from pre-training is that, once you have a learning objective that is sufficiently general and a setup that can absorb more compute and data, scaling tends to keep paying off. The question is whether we can find analogous training paradigms beyond next-token prediction—ways for models to learn from reasoning, interaction, feedback, and eventually their own generated experience—where more scale reliably produces more capable and more robust systems.

Pre-training is unusually clean because the data is abundant and the objective is simple. Post-training is much messier: the feedback is sparse, the environments are harder to build, and it is easier to overfit to what we can measure. But I would expect that as we make those training signals more scalable, the same general phenomenon will reappear: better algorithms matter, but scale lets you turn a small improvement into something qualitatively different.

sol-5.6.text: I think scaling remains the right broad framework, but the thing being scaled may change. Pre-training scaled compute, data, and model size around next-token prediction. Beyond pre-training, the question is whether we can find training signals that let a model spend more computation reasoning, evaluating its own outputs, learning from feedback, and correcting its mistakes. If those methods improve predictably as you give them more compute, then scaling continues—it simply moves from learning from static data to learning through increasingly effective forms of reasoning and feedback.

luna-5.6.text: I think scaling is a much more general principle than just making the pretraining run bigger. Pretraining scales the amount of data and computation used to build a model, but you can also scale the amount of computation used during inference, the amount of reinforcement learning, the number and quality of environments the system experiences, and the amount of search or verification it performs. The important question is whether additional computation produces genuinely better reasoning or better learning, rather than just more fluent output. I expect systems to improve through an iterative process: they generate solutions, check them, learn from the results, and repeat this at larger scale. In that sense, post-training and inference-time computation may eventually become at least as important as pretraining.

luna-6.text: I think of scaling as applying more resources to the whole process of learning, not just making the pre-training run bigger. You can scale the amount of data, the compute, and the quality of the training signal. Beyond pre-training, that might mean more attempts at solving problems, more feedback, or more computation spent on a task at inference time. The key question is whether the extra resources produce a stronger signal that teaches the model something useful. If so, scaling can keep improving performance even when simply adding more text to pre-training gives diminishing returns.
